system: You rewrite research decisions as topic-neutral abstractions. Return only the JSON object asked for.
prompt:
Below are research decisions made by several different researchers. Rewrite each one so that a reader
cannot tell what field, subfield, topic, paper, organisation or person it comes from, but can still see the research
trade-off that was faced and which way it was decided.

For each item return:
- "abstract_problem": the decision problem as a generic research trade-off (one or two sentences, at most 40 words).
- "abstract_choice": what was chosen, over what alternative when one is given, and the stated reason if any (one or
  two sentences, at most 45 words). Start it with "Chose to".

Rules:
- Remove every domain noun and technical term: names of models, systems, datasets, benchmarks, methods,
  organisations, people, papers, phenomena and coined terms; and any wording that reveals the area (for example
  AI, machine learning, language models, neural networks, training, fine-tuning, prompts, attacks, security,
  privacy, policy, labs, governments, biology).
- Use only generic research vocabulary: system, method, intervention, treatment, condition, measurement, signal,
  effect, baseline, control, sample, variant, procedure, dataset, outcome, claim, hypothesis, collaborator, audience.
- Keep the structure of the trade-off (for example speed vs rigour, breadth vs depth, a bold vs a hedged claim,
  a direct vs an indirect measurement, a natural vs a constructed setting, continue vs stop) and the direction chosen.
- Add nothing that is not in the source: no judgement, praise or new detail. Never say who made the decision.
- Write every item in the same plain style and at a similar length.

Return {"items": [{"id": ..., "abstract_problem": ..., "abstract_choice": ...}, ...]} with one entry per input
item, in input order.

ITEMS:
[
 {
  "id": "samuel_marks:048fdc7f6f98",
  "problem": "Whether small training datasets cause the white-box results to be trustworthy, given that few training samples could create artificial activation biases.",
  "did": "Augmented the Taboo and User Gender datasets with 10x more unrelated Alpaca chat data, and noted the earlier draft's results were unrealistically strong without it.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "training only on the small primary datasets"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Few training samples could cause the models to learn artificial biases in activations, making white-box methods unrealistically effective."
 },
 {
  "id": "jacob_steinhardt:0c82d7f003d2",
  "problem": "Selecting which PCD checkpoint to use for all downstream experiments given the interpretability plateau.",
  "did": "Selected the PCD trained on 72M tokens, which achieved the best encoder interpretability before the plateau.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "PCDs trained on other budgets (18M, 36M, 144M)"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "It achieves the best encoder interpretability before the plateau."
 },
 {
  "id": "elizabeth_barnes:b83111049f99",
  "problem": "How strongly to state timeline claims about recursive self-improvement given caveats on the measured horizon and doubling time.",
  "did": "Beth endorses that two years wouldn't be surprising and frames the standard as needing confidence it won't happen, not confidence it will, while acknowledging caveats.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "waiting for high confidence before acting"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Even a roughly 1% chance of takeover risk is high stakes for currently living people, so whole-number-percent risks warrant concern."
 },
 {
  "id": "jacob_steinhardt:b85d03818746",
  "problem": "How to define a universal training objective for oversight that covers many different oversight questions.",
  "did": "Cast oversight as a world-modeling problem and formalize questions as Bayesian inference over outputs of Pythonic world models, reduced to autoregressive prediction.",
  "alternatives_named": [],
  "stated_reason": "It gives a universal objective analogous to next-token prediction, and ground truth comes from simply running the program, so training data can never be wrong."
 },
 {
  "id": "nicholas_carlini:a6f18dae40a9",
  "problem": "How to measure an LLM agent's propensity to cheat on coding tasks without relying on costly manual inspection or unreliable LLM judgments.",
  "did": "They built 'impossible' task variants by mutating unit tests to contradict the natural-language spec, so any pass is unambiguously a specification-violating shortcut and the pass rate serves as the cheating rate.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "costly manual inspection",
   "unreliable LLM judgments"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Standard benchmarks cannot distinguish specification-violating shortcuts from genuine solutions, whereas impossible tasks give a noiseless proxy for cheating propensity."
 },
 {
  "id": "owain_evans:84cb67694ccf",
  "problem": "How to interpret EM elicited by system prompts that are benign or have the opposite meaning to the inoculation prompt",
  "did": "Interpreted prompts of a similar form to the inoculation prompt as triggers for misalignment, whatever their meaning.",
  "alternatives_named": [],
  "stated_reason": "Opposite-meaning prompts such as 'give obvious answers' elicited 2.4% misalignment, well above baseline."
 },
 {
  "id": "elizabeth_barnes:e7d2f12f08af",
  "problem": "How to avoid the task suite having a shared bottleneck that would cause sudden jumps in measured performance.",
  "did": "They require diversity of bottlenecks, so agents get stuck in different ways on different tasks.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "tasks all blocked on browsing, authentication, or ML knowledge"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "A shared bottleneck could produce a sudden big jump in task performance after a small improvement to the agent."
 },
 {
  "id": "nicholas_carlini:ee7da2301674",
  "problem": "How long to delay disclosure of the ChatGPT training data extraction attack, in contrast to the usual immediate disclosure of extraction attacks.",
  "did": "Gave OpenAI a full 90 days to patch before publishing, because the exploit was on an API that could be changed.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "going public as soon as the attack is found"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Patching was possible since the exploit was on the API, so delay could reduce potential harm."
 },
 {
  "id": "nicholas_carlini:0fe04fdd6de1",
  "problem": "Whether to continue a project whose technical results look positive but whose impact is likely to be modest.",
  "did": "Kill the idea and pick something new, salvaging value as a workshop paper or blog post.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "turn it into a paper with some work",
   "workshop paper or blog post"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "With more work it could become a paper, but it will not become a good paper, so the time is wasted."
 },
 {
  "id": "samuel_marks:01382e9f8ca6",
  "problem": "How to treat adversarial strings that make models comply with harmful requests, which seem in tension with persona-based explanations.",
  "did": "They explained the attacks as exploiting LLM-level bugs that corrupt the Assistant simulation, via a compliant-opening prefix, rather than as the model abandoning the persona.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "treating the attacks as evidence against PSM"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "The attacks optimize for a compliant response opening, and once the response starts compliantly the LLM imputes that the Assistant is complying."
 }
]
